questions.prompt: You must never overwrite an existing file. Which `FileMode` should you open the `FileStream` with?
options: `FileMode.Create`
`FileMode.CreateNew`
`FileMode.Truncate`
`FileMode.OpenOrCreate`
questions.explanation: `CreateNew` throws if the file exists and otherwise creates a new one, which is the safe choice. `Create` creates a new file or overwrites an existing one.

questions.prompt: A folder holds millions of files and you want to stop after the first few matches. Which method fits better?
options: `Directory.GetFiles`, because it returns a `string[]` with every match at once
`Directory.CreateDirectory`, because it lists files as it creates the folder
`Directory.EnumerateFiles`, because it returns files lazily as you iterate
`File.ReadAllText`, because it reads the whole folder
questions.explanation: `GetFiles` is eager and loads the entire result set into memory. `EnumerateFiles` returns an `IEnumerable<string>` evaluated lazily, which suits huge directories and stopping early.

questions.prompt: When should you use `FileStream` directly rather than `StreamReader` / `StreamWriter`?
options: For binary files such as images or PDFs, because `FileStream` works with bytes
For text files, because `FileStream` handles encodings
For JSON and config files, because `FileStream` reads lines
Never; `StreamReader` / `StreamWriter` handle both bytes and text
questions.explanation: `FileStream` works with bytes and has no encoding handling, so it suits binary files. `StreamReader` / `StreamWriter` work with characters and strings, handle encodings and suit text files like logs or JSON.

questions.prompt: You write lines with a `StreamWriter`, but the file still looks empty. Which behavior explains this?
options: `StreamWriter` only writes when the file already exists
`WriteLine` writes to the console, not to the file
`StreamWriter` writes bytes, so text is not visible
`StreamWriter` buffers content, so it may not be written until `Flush()` or `Close()`
questions.explanation: `StreamWriter` has buffering: content may not be written to the file until `Flush()` or `Close()` (disposing it with `using` closes it).

questions.prompt: You open a file with `FileShare.None`. What can other processes do with it while you hold it?
options: They can read it but not write to it
They can't open it at all
They can delete it
They can read and write it freely
questions.explanation: `FileShare` controls what others may do while you hold the file; `None` means no other process or stream may open it.

options: `ReadLines` returns an `IEnumerable<string>` and reads lazily line by line; `ReadAllText` reads the entire file into one string
`ReadLines` is asynchronous; `ReadAllText` is synchronous
`ReadLines` only works with binary files
There is no difference; both return a `string[]`
questions.explanation: `File.ReadLines` returns an `IEnumerable<string>` that reads lazily line by line, while `File.ReadAllText` reads the entire file and suits small files.
